notes.meaning: Zophar steps forward to speak to Job a second time. He was deeply offended by Job's previous warnings of God's judgment and feels driven to reply right away. This is Zophar's final speech in the entire book.

Zophar admits that he is speaking out of inner turmoil and great haste. Job's words have stirred up his feelings so much that he cannot keep quiet. Instead of pausing for calm reflection, he rushes in to defend his position.

Zophar feels personally insulted by Job's warning that the friends might face God's judgment. He claims that his own inner understanding compels him to answer and correct Job. In his pride, he is sure that his point of view cannot be mistaken.

Zophar appeals to human history from the very beginning of the world. He asks Job if he has forgotten a truth that everyone has supposedly known since man was first created. He believes all ancient wisdom is on his side.

Zophar lays down his main rule, arguing that evil people can only rejoice for a brief moment. He claims that a hypocrite—someone who pretends to love God while living in sin—will soon lose all his happiness. Zophar aims this directly at Job to explain why his fortunes suddenly vanished.

Even if a proud person becomes so wealthy and important that his greatness seems to touch the sky, his success will not last. He may look down on everyone else and think he is completely safe. Yet all that earthly grandeur cannot protect him from sudden ruin.

The proud oppressor will end up completely destroyed and discarded like waste. Those who used to see him in all his glory will look around and wonder where he went. His high position will turn into total shame and swift ruin.

When morning comes, a dream disappears without a trace, and Zophar says the wicked man vanishes just as fast. Like a fleeting night vision, nothing of him remains once judgment falls. His entire life of power is wiped away as if it never existed.
The people who once gazed on him will never see him again. The house and community where he ruled will no longer have any place for him. He is taken away for good, leaving behind an empty space.

The wicked man's children will be left so poor that they must beg for mercy from the very people their father robbed. Or the oppressor himself, crushed by guilt and trouble, will be forced to give back his stolen goods. God's justice turns the tables so that the greedy family loses everything.

Even when a wicked man is young and full of vigor, death can drag him straight down to the grave. His youthful strength cannot keep him alive when God's punishment strikes. He goes to the dust carrying the heavy burden of his sins with him.

Zophar compares sin to a delicious piece of candy that a person rolls under his tongue to make the sweet taste last. The wicked person loves his evil deeds so much that he holds onto them tightly and refuses to let them go. He thinks he can keep his sins secret and enjoy them in private without any harm.

Although sin tastes sweet at first, it soon turns sour and toxic inside the sinner's body. What seemed delightful becomes as deadly as snake venom in his stomach. Zophar warns that evil pleasures always lead to bitter pain and destruction.

The wicked man gulps down stolen wealth like a feast, but he will not get to keep it. His own sick conscience or God's mighty hand will make him vomit it back up. God will force him to disgorge every single thing he took unjustly.

The ill-gotten gains that the wicked man enjoyed will turn out to be deadly cobra poison. What he swallowed for pleasure ends up killing him like a snakebite. His own wickedness becomes the very weapon that destroys his life.

Rivers of honey and thick cream were symbols of rich blessings and prosperity in the ancient world. Zophar says the wicked man will never live to enjoy those peaceful, plentiful gifts. Because he gained wealth by cruelty, he will miss out on the true goodness God gives.

The oppressor will be forced to give back everything he worked to steal before he can even enjoy it. His profits will be taken away to pay back those he wronged. In the end, he will have no joy from any of his trading or hard labor.

God's judgment falls on this man because he crushed the needy and abandoned the helpless. Instead of caring for the poor, he took their houses by force to make himself richer. Zophar describes these crimes to accuse Job of having been a heartless oppressor.

The wicked man's greed was an endless craving that was never satisfied. Because he never knew inner contentment, his treasures will not be able to save him from ruin. All the worldly things he loved so much will slip right through his fingers.

He devoured everything he could find, leaving nothing behind for anyone else. Because of his ruthless greed, his wealth will suddenly collapse and disappear. When he dies, none of his riches will remain for his family to inherit.

Even when the wicked man seems to have more than enough, deep anxiety and distress will crush him. The misery he caused others will bounce back upon his own head. Other wicked or impoverished people will rise up and take everything he owns.

Just when the evil man sits down to satisfy his desires and feast in comfort, God's burning anger will fall on him like a storm. Judgment will strike him while he is still eating, catching him completely off guard. Zophar likely pointed this out to remind Job of how his children died during a feast.

If the sinner manages to run away from an iron sword, a bronze-tipped arrow from a distance will shoot him down instead. There is no escape from God's reach. When a person flees from one disaster, another judgment is already waiting for him.

The shining arrow tears deep into his body, piercing vital organs like the liver. When the deadly weapon is pulled out of his back, he knows his wound cannot be healed. Overwhelming terrors of death grip his heart as his life slips away.

Complete darkness and ruin are kept in store for all his hidden wealth. A mysterious, heavenly fire that no human lit will burn up him and everything left inside his home. Zophar cruelly alludes to the fire from the sky that had burned Job's sheep and servants.

Heaven itself will uncover the secret crimes the wicked man tried to hide, and the earth will rise up to fight against him. The whole created universe turns into a witness against his evil life. Job had appealed to heaven and earth to prove his innocence, but Zophar insists creation will condemn him instead.

All the wealth and property stored in his house will be swept away like a rushing flood. When the day of God's wrath arrives, nothing the sinner hoarded will stay in his hands. Everything he spent his life gathering will simply wash away.

Zophar concludes that this terrible ruin is the settled inheritance God decrees for every wicked person. He is convinced that this is God's unchanging law for all sinners on earth. By saying this, he coldly writes off Job as a hypocrite who is merely getting what he deserves.
